title: RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation

paper.title: RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning.
Beyond rubrics’ usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes.
Together, these components form RISED . Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains. 1 Introduction Training a single LLM agent across diverse interactive environments offers a promising route toward generalist agents ( NVIDIA, 2025a ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Joint training can benefit from transfer across environments and achieve performance comparable to separately trained specialists ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We study joint training on mixed-environment batches, where multiple environments contribute to each policy update ( NVIDIA, 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Within a limited update budget, an important question is which prompt groups to select from the current rollouts to improve joint training. Existing approaches address different aspects of training-data allocation. Curriculum methods typically allocate training across domains or environments ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Zhu et al., 2026b ) , or adjust sample-level priorities using periodically refreshed difficulty estimates ( NVIDIA, 2025b ) . Online selection instead operates on current rollouts and can adapt to the evolving policy, but commonly prioritizes individual examples using local signals such as reward variability or estimated difficulty ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Neither explicitly accounts for relationships between current rollouts from different environments. A second challenge arises from reward-based supervision. Under GRPO, identical rollout rewards provide no within-group reward contrast to distinguish which behaviours should be reinforced. In multi-environment training, all-failure and all-success groups can occur frequently because environments are learned at different rates. In our experiments, they constitute more than half of the candidate prompt groups, leaving substantial training data without a group-relative reward signal. Figure 1 : Overview of RISED . Sec. 2.2 describes the offline rubric discovery. Sec. 2.4 and Sec. 3 describe the selection and distillation, respectively. Together, these form RISED , which uses rubrics to select training data across diverse agentic environments and reuses them for on-policy self-distillation. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar reward signals in multi-environment RL. Reward-level statistics may be too coarse to characterize relationships relevant to cross-environment transfer, while identical rewards provide no within-group reward contrast. Recent work has explored textual feedback, such as rubric-based guidance, as richer supervision than scalar rewards and demonstrated its effectiveness for training LLMs and agents ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We find that rubric-based feedback is useful beyond policy supervision: it can serve as an effective online data-selection signal for capturing cross-environment relationships, while the same annotations can supply complementary supervision for groups with identical rewards ( Bablani et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Concretely, an LLM judge tags each rollout using a shared, predefined rubric vocabulary (Sec. 2.2 ), producing rubric profiles that make rollout behaviours comparable across environments. We also investigate whether rubric profile similarity is informative about cross-environment transfer: our preliminary analysis finds that it correlates more strongly with cross-environment reward improvements than gradient similarity (Sec. 2.3 ). Motivated by this finding, we select prompt groups that align with the overall rubric profile of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected groups (Sec. 2.4 ). Additionally, the same rubric information is reused during post-training. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, yielding additional token-level supervision even when rollout rewards are identical, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes (Sec. 3 ). Together, these components form RISED : R ubr I cs for agentic multi-environment S election and s E lf- D istillation, with an overview of the framework in Fig. 1 . Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments, while component ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of selection and self-distillation. Rubric-based analysis further reveals more frequent positive behaviours than in baseline rollouts, providing an interpretable account of the behavioural changes accompanying these gains. Our contributions are: • We adopt rollout-level rubric profiles as behavioural descriptions (Sec. 2.2 ) and empirically show that rubric similarity correlates more strongly than gradient similarity with cross-environment reward improvements (Sec. 2.3 ). • We propose RISED , a framework for multi-environment agentic RL that uses the same predefined rubric vocabulary across environments for online prompt-group selection and self-distillation. The selection component uses rubric profiles to select prompt groups across environments (Sec. 2.4 ). Positive rubrics condition the self-distillation teacher, while negative rubrics guide subsequent rollout generation (Sec. 3 ). • We conduct extensive experiments and ablations to evaluate RISED across multiple model backbones (Sec. 4.3 ) and demonstrate the complementary benefits of selection and self-distillation. We further use rubric profiles to characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains (Sec. 5 ). 2 Rubrics For Data Selection 2.1 Problem Setup We train a single policy jointly over a set of environments ℰ \mathcal{E} using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Prompts are scheduled for rollout generation in a round-robin manner across environments, targeting a uniform environment mixture, aligned with previous work setting ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . At each training step t t , we construct a candidate batch ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} of rollout groups. Each group g = ( τ g , i ) i = 1 n g=(\tau_{g,i})_{i=1}^{n} contains n n rollouts sharing a prompt x g x_{g} from environment e ⁡ ( g ) ∈ ℰ e(g)\in\mathcal{E} . A rollout τ g , i = ( x g , y g , i ) \tau_{g,i}=(x_{g},y_{g,i}) consists of the prompt and a completion or interaction sequence y g , i y_{g,i} generated by the rollout policy. We oversample by a factor of two, forming | ℬ t | = 2 ​ k |\mathcal{B}_{t}|=2k candidate groups ( 2 ​ k ​ n 2kn rollouts in total), and select a subset 𝒮 t ⊆ ℬ t \mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{t} of | 𝒮 t | = k |\mathcal{S}_{t}|=k groups ( k ​ n kn rollouts) for the policy update. Two properties of this setup are worth emphasizing. First, the choice is made online , once per step, against the current policy, unlike one-time selection of a fixed training subset, which cannot respond to a policy that keeps changing. Second, selecting from a 2 × 2\times candidate pool rather than the full task set bounds the cost: in RL, scoring a candidate usually requires generation, so evaluating the entire pool at every step is not affordable. Generating a surplus and selecting down is a standard compromise in online batch selection ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2015 ; Mindermann et al., 2022 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) , and similar patterns are seen in RL post-training ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . 2.2 Rubric Construction From rubrics as rewards to rubrics as descriptions. Rubrics decompose rollout quality into individually identifiable behaviours and have primarily been used as reward signals for RL ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We repurpose these behavioural descriptions for sample selection, using shared rubric profiles to compare rollouts across environments. Using them as rewards requires careful calibration: every criterion is eventually folded into a scalar ( Tyagi et al., 2026 ) , so a missing or miscalibrated criterion can provide no gradient toward an omitted behaviour, or the wrong one. This requirement is expensive in agentic environments, where a task may admit many successful rollouts and exhaustively specifying in advance the desired good behaviours is difficult. We ask considerably less of the criteria: we identify the prominent behaviours exhibited by each rollout and compare rollouts through these behavioural profiles. 1 1 1 For selection, an incomplete rubric set may make rollouts appear more similar, weakening the signal rather than directly defining an incorrect reward. A more important requirement when using rubrics for selection is consistency across rollouts. The criteria need not exhaustively cover desirable behaviours, but should capture enough variation to distinguish rollouts. Rubric Vocabulary. Each rubric denotes a fine-grained behavioural pattern, represented by a snake_case name. We construct a predefined rubric vocabulary from warm-up model rollouts and augment it with behaviours identified in stronger LLM-generated rollouts. Because warm-up rollouts predominantly end in failure, successful LLM-generated rollouts are introduced to improve coverage of desired behaviours that would otherwise be underrepresented.
